# How to Try New AI Tools Safely (A 5-Minute Beginner's Guide)

You open a shiny new AI app, type in a question, and get an answer that feels a little too specific about you. It happens to everyone. The good news: a handful of small habits keep your experiments fun, useful, and private.

## Why a few safety habits matter

Most AI tools today run on something called an **LLM (large language model — the text-prediction engine behind tools like ChatGPT)**. These models learn from enormous amounts of public text, but anything you type into them can be stored, logged, or used to improve the service. A quick safety routine takes less than five minutes and stops most everyday slip-ups.

## A simple five-step safety routine

### 1. Use a "burner" email when you sign up

Before you hand over your main address, create a free secondary email (think of it like a spare key you only give to strangers). Gmail, Outlook, and Apple's Hide My Email all make this easy. This way, your main inbox stays clean if the tool turns out to be spammy.

### 2. Stick to a separate browser profile

Open a fresh browser profile (Chrome and Edge both have this — it's a clean workspace with its own bookmarks, logins, and cookies) just for AI experiments. Anything you do stays neatly separated from your banking, work, or personal tabs. When you're done experimenting, close the profile.

### 3. Run a "clean input" check before you send

**Prompt sanitisation** — sounds technical, but it just means: before you paste anything into the AI, scan it for sensitive bits. Use this quick checklist:

- Replace your real name with **[YOUR NAME]**
- Replace addresses, phone numbers, and emails with **[REDACTED]**
- Strip out anything that looks like a password, account number, or login link

A sentence like *"My dog Max keeps chewing the cables in my unit at 12 Smith St, Chicago"* becomes *"My dog [PET NAME] keeps chewing cables in my [CITY] unit"*. The AI still helps you. Your details stay yours.

### 4. Watch for three red flags

A healthy chatbot shouldn't:

- Ask you to install software or click a download link
- Offer to "verify your identity" through a third-party site
- Reference personal details you never typed in

If any of these pop up, close the tab. You can report the conversation to the platform through the help menu, which usually has a "report" or "safety" link.

### 5. Wipe the conversation when you're done

Most AI tools keep a chat history. When you've finished experimenting, look for a **"clear conversation"** or **"delete chat"** option (usually a small trash icon or three-dot menu near the chat). Doing this once a week keeps old prompts from piling up.

## What this means for you

- **If you're just curious about a new chatbot**: Use a spare email, a separate browser profile, and the clean-input checklist. You'll be safe in under five minutes.
- **If you use AI for work or study**: Keep your AI experiments in that separate browser profile, never paste client or student data, and clear conversations at the end of each session.
- **If you've already shared something sensitive**: Don't panic. Go into the chat history, delete the conversation, and from now on use the redaction habit. Most modern platforms also let you request full data deletion from your account settings.

## Wrap-up

Trying new AI tools should feel exciting, not risky. With a spare email, a clean browser profile, a 30-second input checklist, awareness of red flags, and a habit of clearing old chats, you've got a complete safety routine. Today, pick one new AI tool you've been curious about, sign up with your spare email, and run your first test prompt using the redaction checklist above. You'll have a safer setup before your coffee gets cold.
